To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the grain size of the data used to represent biodiversity patterns is an important issue for conservation planning and can have a large effect on planning outcomes; (ii) this is especially true when planning for rare species, where a mismatch between the coarse representation of biodiversity patterns and small areas of actual occupancy is more pronounced; and (iii) conservation planning is sensitive to the grain size of data, which is a key issue that has been neglected so far in conservation planning.

the grain size of the spatial representation of species distribution data can have an important effect on conservation outcomes, and the use of coarse data can result in an important increase in the risk of misallocation and commission errors, particularly for rare species.
conservation uncertainty increases as the grain size of data used in conservation planning increases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the importance of using the appropriate grain size of species data for conservation planning, and the implications of not doing so.
the need for a better representation of the spatial patterns of biodiversity in order to improve the efficiency of conservation investments.
the effect of the grain size of species data on conservation planning performance and highlights the need for a more thorough consideration of the grain size effect on conservation planning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of the grain size of species distributions is more important than the effect of planning unit size for the conservation of species.
the grain size of species distributions should be as fine as possible to achieve the best conservation outcomes.
planning at coarse grain size should be avoided.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the grain size of species occurrence data should be considered as important as the grain size of planning units when planning for biodiversity conservation, and that coarse species distribution data may not be suitable for planning at small spatial scale or for the conservation of rare species.
coarse conservation assessments can be highly misleading, and the use of fine-scale species distribution data is a prerequisite for effective conservation planning.

the effect of the scale at which we represent species distribution is more important than the scale at which planning is done, and should be carefully considered when undertaking conservation planning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
conservation planners should be cautious when using coarse representations of species distribution data, and should be aware of the potential consequences for conservation planning.
conservation planning should be based on high-resolution data, even when planning for large-scale conservation.

conservation planners should be aware of the grain of the species data they use and that the effect of planning unit size is less important than the mismatch between grain size of species data and the scale of conservation units.
